title: When the Post Office Can't Read Your Handwriting #shorts
summary: USPS machines read about 98% of handwritten addresses. The rest go as photos to the last Remote Encoding Center in Salt Lake City, where 730+ people key about 2.3 million addresses a day, around the clock.
sources: The Advanced Facer Canceller System positions letters and postmarks stamps at 36,000 pieces an hour; machines read nearly 98 percent of hand-addressed letters and 99.5 percent of machine-printed mail; the Intelligent Mail barcode identifies individual pieces so they can be tracked (USPS Postal Facts, Innovation): https://facts.usps.com/innovation/

Remote Encoding Center, Salt Lake City: about 2.3 million address images a day, more than 730 employees, open 24/7; 55 centers at the late-1990s peak, the only one since 2014 (USPS Link, 23 Apr 2024): https://news.usps.com/2024/04/23/the-postal-services-digital-detectives-are-marking-a-milestone/

scenes.narration: Machines read about {98%|ninety-eight percent} of handwritten addresses. If yours is in the other two percent, a photo of your envelope goes to Salt Lake City.
There, more than {730|seven hundred thirty} people type in about {2.3 million|two point three million} addresses a day.
They work around the clock, so your letter barely stops moving.
In the late {1990s|nineties} there were {55|fifty-five} centers like this. Now it's the last one.
